summary:
Daniel Chalef addresses the engineering challenge of maintaining provenance in knowledge graphs built by LLMs. Because LLMs synthesize data non-deterministically, output artifacts often do not appear verbatim in source inputs, destroying the paper trail of how facts were generated. Simple source IDs fail because LLM pipelines merge entities (e.g., J. Smith and John Smith) and invalidate old facts with new data, causing the store to mutate under the pointer. Chalef presents Graphiti, the open-source temporal graph framework behind Zep, which models source data as "episodes" and facts as edges between extracted entities. In this model, tracing a fact to its origin is a simple graph walk.

When entities merge, the merged entity retains all source links to prevent silent lineage loss. When new data contradicts old data, Graphiti adds an invalid date to the mutated edge and notes the responsible episodes. Metadata projection allows sources to be tagged once at ingestion (e.g., an "EHR" tag), with all derived entities and facts inheriting the tag, enabling agents to filter by veracity. For facts with multiple parent episodes, business rules determine if partial verification suffices (e.g., allergy flags) or if all parents must be verified (e.g., procedural consent).

Deletion for GDPR or retention policies leverages the same lineage graph. When an episode is deleted, a derived fact survives only if other supporting episodes remain. Chalef highlights that while provenance offers compliance, veracity, and debuggability, graph construction is expensive. Graphiti mitigates this by using traditional NLP techniques like simhash and entropy analysis for deduplication and deconfliction, reserving LLMs for specific extraction tasks. In Q&A, Chalef notes that weight-based relevancy mutations are handled in Zep using a separate data structure. He also explains that markdown or file-based memory breaks down for provenance because mutating lines in files obscures lineage, and managing markdown at scale is challenging in multi-agent, multi-user, multi-source enterprise scenarios. Graphiti uses single-shot LLM extraction for entities, relationships, and facts, keeping costs low, with a reflection step ensuring accuracy and enriching lineage to capture why changes occurred.

sections.title: Introduction and the Provenance Problem
sections.summary: Daniel Chalef introduces the challenge of provenance in LLM-built knowledge graphs, noting that LLMs non-deterministically synthesize data and destroy paper trails. He introduces Graphiti and Zep as solutions and presents a healthcare failure mode where a penicillin allergy fact synthesized from three sources lacks clear origin, potentially misleading a doctor.

sections.title: Why Source IDs Fail and Provenance as a Graph
sections.summary: Chalef explains why simple source IDs fail due to entity merging and fact mutation. He presents Graphiti's model: sources are episodes, entities are extracted, and facts are edges. Tracing a fact is a graph walk. When entities merge, all source links are retained; when facts are mutated, invalid dates and source episodes are noted.

sections.title: Metadata Projection and Mixed Trust Policies
sections.summary: Metadata projection allows tagging episodes at ingestion (e.g., "EHR"), with derived facts inheriting tags for veracity filtering. Chalef discusses mixed trust parents, where business rules dictate whether one verified source suffices (allergy flag) or all sources must be verified (consent).

sections.title: Deletion, Benefits, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Chalef explains GDPR erasure as a reverse graph walk: deleting an episode only deletes a fact if no remaining episodes support it. He lists benefits: compliance, veracity, and debuggability, and notes Graphiti is open-source.

sections.title: Q&A: Mutation, Extraction, Markdown, and Reflection
sections.summary: In Q&A, Chalef clarifies that weight-based relevancy is handled in Zep, not Graphiti, using a separate data structure. He explains that episodes are graph nodes, and the add episode pipeline runs structured extraction followed by deduplication and deconfliction using traditional NLP techniques like simhash to reduce costs. When asked about markdown and file-based memory, he argues these break down for provenance because file mutations obscure lineage and markdown is hard to manage at scale in multi-agent, multi-user, multi-source enterprise scenarios. On fact creation, he explains Graphiti uses single-shot LLM extraction for entities, relationships, and facts cheaply, with a reflection step ensuring accuracy and enriching lineage to capture why changes occurred, split partly between Graphiti and Zep.

demonstrations: Stylized healthcare failure mode where a penicillin allergy is synthesized from three sources (EHR, lab report, intake chat).
Example of metadata tagging where episodes are tagged "EHR" at ingestion and derived facts inherit the tag for filtering.
Mixed trust policy example contrasting allergy flags (one verified parent) with consent facts (all parents verified).
Deletion example where an intake chat episode is deleted, but the allergy fact survives due to other supporting episodes, while a contact preference fact is deleted.
Graph mutation example where "Daniel loves Adidas shoes" is invalidated by "Daniel returned shoes" through deconfliction.
limitations: Weight changes in relevancy for graph edges are not built into Graphiti but handled by Zep using a separate data structure.
Markdown or file-based memory breaks down with provenance, especially in multi-agent, multi-user, multi-source enterprise scenarios.
Reflection step for lineage richness is split partly between Graphiti and Zep, not fully in one component.
quantitativeClaims: Graph construction is expensive in the way Graphiti does it.
Single-shot extraction enables cheap entity, relationship, and fact extraction using an LLM.
